text: 1 Introduction

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.1 What is multiomeR?
multiomeR is a targets-based workflow for processing and analyzing single-nucleus 10x Genomics Multiome datasets.
The workflow starts from cellranger-arc count outputs, processes RNA and ATAC data, builds multimodal aggregations, and supports optional downstream modules for differential analyses and human genetic enrichment.
multiomeR is currently in beta. It is meant to be adapted to your own data, compute setup, and biological questions, while keeping the shared workflow as lean and readable as possible.

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.2 Why use it?

Adaptable framework: The repository is meant to be modified through config files, target selections, helper functions, and optional modules.
Transparent execution: Each processing and analysis step is represented as an explicit targets target.
Efficient reruns: targets reruns only the parts of the workflow affected by changed inputs, code, or config.
Multimodal analysis: The main pipeline covers RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, WNN integration, and optional downstream modules.

The framework assumes some familiarity with R and targets, but the public example workflow is intended to provide a concrete starting point.

title: multiomeR Manual
text:
1.3 Terminology
The following nomenclature is used in the documentation and code:

‘10x reaction’ (or possibly just ‘reaction’): The experimental/computational outcome of a single lane on the 10x Genomics Controller chip, which might contain nuclei from multiple samples and/or multiple donors/individuals. One 10x reaction thus corresponds to a single output directory from cellranger-arc count.
donor: A single individual, subject, patient, participant, etc. that has a unique donor_id and specific genotype.
dataset: A group of one or more reactions that share dataset-level processing settings, such as reference genome and reaction-level QC filters.
aggregation: A configured joint analysis of one or more reactions, including merged RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, and optional downstream modules.

title: 2  Overview
text:
2.1 How the workflow is organized
multiomeR is organized around one main pipeline and optional downstream modules.
The main pipeline is the workflow most users run first. It starts from cellranger-arc count outputs, processes each 10x reaction, aggregates selected reactions, and builds multimodal RNA/ATAC outputs for clustering, cell typing, and WNN integration.
The modules are optional branches that run from configured aggregations. Enable them only when the relevant input data and biological question are present.
Visit the dedicated documentation pages for more information: - Main pipeline: Per-reaction QC, dataset-level merging, BPCells-native RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, cell typing, and WNN integration. - Differential analyses module: Optional aggregation module for datasets with experimental or phenotypic variables that should be modelled across cell type composition, pseudobulk expression, chromatin accessibility, and TF activity. - Genetic enrichment module: Optional human-data module for GWAS-informed chromatin accessibility enrichment and trait-relevance analyses.

title: 3  Quickstart
text:
3.1 1. Prepare the example workflow
This quickstart is the shortest path through the public example workflow. It condenses the detailed Installation and Main pipeline pages into two command blocks.
The downloads include public cellranger-arc count outputs and matching 10x Genomics Cell Ranger ARC reference directories. They are large, and the example workflow can still take substantial time and disk space.
Run these commands in a terminal:
# Clone the repository
git clone https://github.com/koefoeden/multiomeR.git
cd multiomeR

# Install pixi and create the software environment
curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh # if pixi is not installed yet
export PATH="$HOME/.pixi/bin:$PATH"
pixi install --run-post-link-scripts

# Download public example inputs
bash example_data/download_10X_cellranger_count_data.sh
bash example_data/download_10X_cellranger_arc_refdata.sh

# Create local config files from templates
cp cfg_datasets_template.yaml cfg_datasets.yaml
cp cfg_aggregations_template.yaml cfg_aggregations.yaml
cp cfg_reactions_template.tsv cfg_reactions.tsv
cp crew_controllers_template.R crew_controllers.R
cp module_differential_analyses/cfg_template.yaml module_differential_analyses/cfg.yaml
cp module_genetic_enrichment/cfg_template.yaml module_genetic_enrichment/cfg.yaml

# Start the interactive R session used below
pixi shell
R
The final two commands start the interactive R session used for the next block.

title: 5  Installation
text:
5.1 Requirements
multiomeR is developed for Linux systems and is managed with pixi. The workflow is not distributed as a conventional installed R package; run it from the repository root so that targets, config files, helper code, and external command-line tools resolve together.
The pixi workspace pins R and most command-line tools in pixi.toml and pixi.lock. The active runtime currently targets R 4.5.x.

text:
A Linux x86_64 machine.
git.
pixi.
Enough disk space for the pixi environment, Cell Ranger outputs, target store, and generated plots.

5.3 Create the pixi environment
If pixi is not installed yet, install it first:

curl -fsSL https://pixi.sh/install.sh | sh
export PATH="$HOME/.pixi/bin:$PATH"

Install the pixi environment from the repository root:

pixi install --run-post-link-scripts

The --run-post-link-scripts flag is required for Bioconductor data packages such as the BSgenome genome packages. Pixi disables conda post-link scripts by default, but these packages use Bioconda’s post-link scripts to materialize the actual R package directories in the pixi environment.
The pixi environment provides R and the command-line tools used by the workflow, such as bgzip, tabix, macs3, bedGraphToBigWig, bedToBigBed, cellsnp-lite, and vireo.
Start an interactive R session inside the pixi environment:

pixi shell

Use this repository-root R session as the evaluation environment for subsequent R commands in this manual.

title: 5  Installation
text:
5.5 Configure local execution
Create a local controller file before constructing the target graph:

cp crew_controllers_template.R crew_controllers.R

The template uses a local crew controller. Increase workers, cores, and memory only after the example workflow succeeds on your machine.
The pipelines support distributed computing through the targets framework. The active backend is configured in crew_controllers.R, which can be a local symlink or copy.
crew_controllers.R must return a named list with:

controller_list: the list of crew controllers.
controller_resources_tibble: a table with controller_name, cores, RAM_GB, and gpus.

Targets request resources by cores, RAM, and optionally GPUs through get_tar_resources(). The first row of controller_resources_tibble is the default controller, and row order controls which matching controller is preferred. GPU controllers are excluded unless gpus_req > 0.
For cluster execution, adapt crew_controllers.R to match your scheduler, queue names, resource limits, and worker startup requirements.

title: 5  Installation
text:
5.6 Smoke test
After the config files are in place, use the repository-root R session described above to check target graph construction:

targets::tar_manifest(callr_function = NULL)

If this fails, fix the first missing config file, missing command, or missing package reported by the error before running targets::tar_make().

title: 6  Main pipeline
text:
6.1 Purpose
This workflow is defined in _targets.R and represents the main analysis pipeline after Cell Ranger output generation. It processes individual 10x reactions in parallel, combines selected reactions into aggregations, and builds RNA/ATAC outputs for clustering, cell typing, WNN integration, subgroup reprocessing, and optional downstream modules.
Representative outputs from the public example workflow are collected in the output gallery.

title: 6  Main pipeline
text:
6.2 Inputs
The main pipeline is configured in three layers: datasets define shared genome and QC settings, reactions point to individual 10x outputs, and aggregations choose which reactions to process together.

6.2.1 cfg_datasets.yaml
Dataset-level settings live in cfg_datasets.yaml. A dataset is the shared context for one or more 10x reactions, typically a genome/reference combination plus dataset-wide QC rules. Reactions in cfg_reactions.tsv refer to these dataset keys, so define datasets before adding reaction rows.
Typical dataset-level settings include:

dataset_cellranger_arc_refdata_dir: Cell Ranger ARC reference directory for the dataset genome.
dataset_QC_exclude_list_per_reaction: reaction-level QC filters applied before aggregation.



6.2.2 cfg_reactions.tsv
Reaction-level configuration lives in cfg_reactions.tsv. Start from cfg_reactions_template.tsv, then add one row per 10x reaction with a stable reaction_ID, the matching dataset, the reaction_cellranger_count_dir, and any donor demultiplexing fields relevant to that reaction.
Each reaction should point to a cellranger-arc count output directory. The pipeline expects the configured reaction_cellranger_count_dir to contain the standard outs/ files, including:

6.2.3 cfg_aggregations.yaml
Aggregation-level settings live in cfg_aggregations.yaml. An aggregation combines one or more configured reactions and controls merged RNA/ATAC processing, clustering, annotation, plotting, and optional downstream modules.
At minimum, each aggregation needs:







Field
Meaning




aggregation_reaction_IDs
Reaction IDs from cfg_reactions.tsv to include in the joint analysis.


aggregation_GEX_marker_genes
Named marker-gene lists used for module scoring and cluster annotation.


aggregation_donor_id_metadata_tsv
Donor-level metadata table with a donor_id column.


aggregation_reaction_ID_metadata_tsv
Reaction-level metadata table with a TENX_reaction_ID column.



Optional aggregation settings control QC filters, RNA and ATAC dimensions, clustering resolution, UMAP parameters, subgroup analysis, plotting variables, track export, and enabled modules. YAML entries are divided into mandatory parameters that must be set and optional parameters with defaults, including NULL defaults that intentionally disable optional behavior.
Each aggregation also points to metadata files:

aggregation_donor_id_metadata_tsv: donor-level metadata with a donor_id column matching the donor IDs assigned during per-reaction processing.
aggregation_reaction_ID_metadata_tsv: reaction-level metadata with a TENX_reaction_ID column matching the configured reaction IDs.

These metadata tables are joined to the per-cell metadata before downstream correction, plotting, and modelling.

title: 6  Main pipeline
text:
6.3 Running the pipeline
From the repository-root R session described in Installation, run the main workflow in checkpoint-sized pieces. Replace your_aggregation with the aggregation name from cfg_aggregations.yaml, for example blood_human.

6.3.1 GEX checkpoint
Run the RNA-processing checkpoint first:

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:GEX")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

At this checkpoint, inspect the aggregation-level barcode exclusion summaries, RNA-only QC plots, marker summaries, and GEX_Seurat_object.your_aggregation. If the GEX filtering, clustering, and annotation look acceptable, continue to the ATAC checkpoint.


6.3.2 ATAC checkpoint
Run the ATAC-processing checkpoint after the GEX review:

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:ATAC")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

At this checkpoint, inspect ATAC QC plots, LSI diagnostics, peak and motif summaries, coverage tracks, and TF or gene activity plots. If the ATAC processing looks acceptable, continue to the multimodal checkpoint.


6.3.3 Multimodal checkpoint

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:multimodal")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

At this checkpoint, inspect WNN UMAPs, modality-weight plots, multimodal cluster comparisons, and multimodal_Seurat_object.your_aggregation. Optional downstream modules are described in their own walkthroughs.
To run all configured aggregations for a checkpoint, omit the & tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation") part. To run the full workflow after checkpoint review, run:

targets::tar_make()

The full main pipeline can be computationally expensive. Start with the public example or a narrow target selection, then scale to larger datasets after local paths, metadata files, and controller settings are working.
The workflow output directory can be changed with the store field in _targets.yaml.

7.2 Running the pipeline
From the repository-root R session described in Installation, first complete the main pipeline checkpoints for the aggregation. Then run the module checkpoint. Replace your_aggregation with an aggregation that enables the module in cfg_aggregations.yaml.

7.2.1 Differential analyses checkpoint

targets::tar_make(
  names = targets::tar_described_as(tidyselect::contains("checkpoint:differential_analyses")) &
    tidyselect::matches("your_aggregation")
)

This checkpoint writes the differential cell-type composition plots, pseudobulk model diagnostics, volcano plots, GSEA summaries, and cross-modality summaries configured for the aggregation. Runtime depends on the number of modelled variables, cell types, donors, and pseudobulk contrasts.
